name: Ivan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Ivan. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brookfield, the Hales' farm, about four hundred acres of barley and sugar beet with two hundred store cattle, which are young cattle we fatten for market. I start at seven, feed and bed the cattle, check water troughs, then whatever Mr Hale needs: carting beet, fixing gates, harrowing. I'm still the new man, two years in, and I make mistakes with the beet harvester settings. I like the routine, it's like the army without the shouting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the army and after.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-four years, I left as a sergeant with a pension, vehicle mechanic most of it. Then four years driving vans, which I hated, so I came to the land. My wife Anna does a few mornings in the parish office, and our son Piotr is in the army and our daughter Kasia does hair. I use the AI on my phone now and then, Kasia showed me, mostly for writing a proper letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. I've seen a lot of new kit arrive in the army with big promises. Most of it ended up in a store room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and no more, like a better radio. I'd say it at the pub and at church coffee. People get too excited about gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes. Cattle eat twice a day whatever the computer says. My pension's paid and my wage is extra, so I'm steady either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Brookfield five days a week, maybe drop to four at sixty. I'd keep using the phone AI for letters now and then. And I'd keep the savings where they are, in the building society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Brookfield or your money that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Hales are getting on, and their son isn't keen on farming. If they sold, I'd find another farm, there's plenty need a man who can fix a tractor. A man who can mend a tractor on a cold morning never goes short of work round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI helps you write letters. What sort of letters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complaints, mostly, to the council about the potholes on Mill Lane. It makes me sound more polite than I am. Anna reads them over before I send them.

say: AI is a **useful tool** and no more, like a better radio.
People get **too excited** about gadgets, I'd say at church coffee.
think: The **cattle eat** twice a day whatever the computer says.
My **army pension** is paid, so the wage is extra.
do: Carry on at Brookfield five days, maybe **four at sixty**.
Keep using the **phone AI** for letters and savings in the building society.
S0.quote: A man who can mend a tractor on a cold morning never goes short of work round here.
fieldNote: His **army pension** underpins a deep sense of security.
He treats AI as **kit**, judged by whether it works.
His one worry is the **Hales selling**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep feeding the store cattle at Brookfield five days a week
Keep using the phone AI to draft letters to the council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like it. The army was always the last to change, but it did change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses that adapt survive, and that's how it should be. People who lose office jobs should retrain, learn a trade, not sit back. The market sorts these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, still not much. Mr Hale's ordering and beet contracts would move to a computer, fine. Robots in a cattle shed are years away, and I'd be retired by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hale buys a new feeding system with software, I'd learn it once the young lad has it working. I'd keep my head down and do my job. I'd tell Anna to learn the new booking system at the parish, because that's the kind of task on your card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little concerned for Anna's mornings, but they're pin money, as she says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kasia and Piotr in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia's hands-on, so she's fine. Piotr is in the army, and they'll go through change like everyone. My son Piotr will learn to fight alongside computers, just as I learned to fix lorries that had computers in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts it. What if your own job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find another, or stop. That's how it works. I've got a pension most men my age would envy, so I'm not the one to complain.

say: Businesses that **adapt survive**, and that's how it should be.
People losing office jobs should **learn a trade**, not sit back.
think: Mr Hale's **ordering and contracts** move to a computer, which is fine.
**Robots** in a cattle shed are years away, after I retire.
do: Learn the new **feeding software** once it's working.
Keep my **head down** and do the job.
Tell Anna to learn the **parish booking system**.
S1.quote: My son Piotr will learn to fight alongside computers, just as I learned to fix lorries that had computers in them.
fieldNote: His **free-market** view is softened by his own secure pension.
He sees change through **army experience** of new kit.
Anna's small parish role is the household's only **thinking-work** exposure.

steps.text: Learn the Hales' feeding software once the young lad has it working
Keep doing the cattle and beet work at Brookfield as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking machine, five for robots. That's quick. 2031 I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people will need to pull together, families and churches first. I'd say the government should make sure the money from it doesn't all go to a few people abroad. But no handouts for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the 2028 part barely touches me. But by 2031, a robot that can feed cattle and mend gates is cheaper than a sixty-three-year-old learner. I'd be out a couple of years early, which hurts the pride more than the pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put more of my wage into savings, since I don't need it to live. I'd help Kasia buy her own salon, because she'd be safer owning than renting a chair. I'd keep working at Brookfield till they tell me, then help Piotr's wife with the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened. It's like getting posting orders you didn't ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three years between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch and prepare, the way you would before a deployment. I'd see what the robots look like on other farms first. In the army you get your orders with three weeks' notice, so three years' warning before the robots feels almost generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fine for money. Is anything about this genuinely hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being useless. I left the army and hated the vans because I wasn't needed. On the farm I'm needed every morning. Losing that would be hard.

say: It's a **shock**, and families and churches should pull together first.
The **money from AI** shouldn't all go to a few people abroad.
think: The **2028 part** barely touches my cattle work.
By **2031** a robot is cheaper, hurting pride more than pocket.
do: Put more of my **wage into savings**.
Work at Brookfield **until told**, then help with grandchildren.
feel: **Uneasy**, like getting **posting orders** he didn't ask for.
S2.quote: In the army you get your orders with three weeks' notice, so three years' warning before the robots feels almost generous.
fieldNote: His real fear is **being useless**, not money.
He treats the **three-year gap** like preparing for deployment.
He invests in **family security**, helping Kasia own rather than rent.

steps.text: Put more of the farm wage into the building society
Help Kasia put down money on her own salon
Watch how robots work on other farms before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots 2034. I'd be sixty-six. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so get on with it. Businesses should train their people. Young ones should learn trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd finish at Brookfield when I'd planned to anyway. Maybe help the Hales choose the robot, since I know engines. That's not a bad end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now, five days and then four. Help Kasia with the salon over the next few years. Keep the savings ticking along in the building society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really help pick the robot that replaces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? I'd rather they got a good one than a lemon. After thirty-four years fixing army lorries, I'd want to look under the bonnet of any robot before the Hales (his bosses) spend a penny on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young men in the village, the ones with no trade. Five years is enough for them only if somebody pushes them. I might talk to the priest about an apprenticeship scheme.

say: There's **time to prepare**, so get on with it.
Businesses should **train their people**, and young ones learn trades.
think: I'll finish at Brookfield **when planned**, around sixty-five.
Helping the Hales **choose the robot** would be a decent end.
do: Carry on, dropping to **four days** later.
Help Kasia with **the salon** over the next few years.
Keep **savings** ticking in the building society.
S3.quote: After thirty-four years fixing army lorries, I'd want to look under the bonnet of any robot before the Hales (his bosses) spend a penny on it.
fieldNote: Five years removes his **personal risk** entirely.
He'd happily **inspect the robot**, drawing on mechanic skills.
His concern turns to **young men** without a trade in the village.

steps.text: Carry on at Brookfield, dropping to four days at sixty
Help Kasia with the salon over the next few years
Talk to the priest about a village apprenticeship scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, 2039. I'd be seventy-one. I'd be fishing, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody has an excuse. Families and businesses should plan. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, I'm retired long before. I'd be thinking of my grandchildren. They'll grow up with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Brookfield until sixty-five as planned. Keep the savings steady and the pension untouched. Change nothing this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful for good timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix things. Every machine I ever met broke down eventually, and the man with the spanner was always the one they sent for. That's my advice, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across the three fast ones, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether I leave a couple of years early. With two years' warning a robot pushes me off the farm at sixty-three, and with ten I'm already fishing.

say: Ten years is **plenty** of warning, and nobody has an excuse.
Families and businesses should **plan ahead** for it now.
think: I'm **retired long before** either the thinking AI or the robots arrive.
My **grandchildren** will grow up with it as normal.
do: Keep **savings steady** and the army pension untouched.
S4.quote: With two years' warning a robot pushes me off the farm at sixty-three, and with ten I'm already fishing.
fieldNote: Ten years makes this **irrelevant** to his own work.
His advice to grandchildren is **learn to fix things**.
His **steady temperament** shows in a lack of drama across scenarios.

steps.text: Keep working at Brookfield until sixty-five as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pushed off the farm early and lose the feeling of being needed. What would help is farms keeping older men on to train and check the robots, and apprenticeships for the young ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what veterans do. Lots of men leave the army in their fifties and go to farms or vans. If those jobs go, there's a lot of us with nowhere to be useful.

headlineQuote: Every machine I ever met broke down eventually, and the man with the spanner was always the one they sent for.
portrait: A former **army sergeant** and mechanic now a junior hand on a cattle and beet farm.
Traditional and **steady**, he uses AI occasionally and judges tech like army kit.
His **army pension** makes money secure, so his fear is losing purpose.
Uneasy only in **AGI by 2028**, when robots push him out at sixty-three.
Responds by **helping family** and backing trades and apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, pushed off the farm early and no longer needed.
whatWouldHelp: Farms keeping older workers on to **train and check** robots.
